title: How do the parts fit the whole?- the role of seemingly vague facts ly-vague-facts/
author: Jo Castelino
summary: Castelino, a biology teacher, follows an earlier post on checking understanding by asking what to do when the parts of a course are small, seemingly vague facts that recur across many later topics. Her argument is that a single lesson cannot reveal the thread, so teachers must repeatedly reattach significance to such facts as the course unfolds. She uses the cell membrane and cytoplasm as worked examples, tracing how the membrane reappears in semi-permeability, diffusion, villi and microvilli, and respiration. She admits her earlier practice was to state a structure's job and move on, leaving it meaningless to students. She closes with four benefits: facts gain meaning, simple facts are retrieved often, students build schemas, and later learning is easier to build.
points: Simple facts like the function of the cell membrane stay inert unless teachers repeatedly tie them to the larger processes where they matter.
Planting a seed early (substances need a way through) and returning to it at diffusion, villi and respiration builds a thread across the whole course.
The practice costs little time; it is about attaching meaning to a function rather than relaying the definition each time.
The author frames the method as retrieval plus schema-building: students recall simple facts often and link them to major ideas in memory.
She models honest reflection by naming her own past mistake of stating a structure's job without its significance.
quotes: To make the thread running through a course become apparent to our novice learners, we have to reiterate the significance and links connecting a seemingly vague fact to other ideas/facts.

One mistake that I would make is to not explain the significance of all relevant structures in a cell to processes. Sure, I would say that a certain structure does a certain job and that would be that. There was no actual meaning to it.
When teaching the cell membrane initially, I make sure to suggest that substances need a way to pass through and not just to say that is its job. I am planting a seed that I will return to later.
The cell membrane has a role to play in many major processes but its very structure enables certain processes to happen at increased rates.

Here, I explain that microvilli are folds or protusions of the cell membrane of the cells that make up the villi. Having the larger surface area means more digested food molecules can pass through quickly. This makes the rate of diffusion higher and the whole thing very efficient.

None of this takes a lot of time. In fact, in some cases, many teachers already mention the cell membrane. But this is more about attaching meaning to its function and not just relaying the definition each time.

A similar process can be followed when teaching the cytoplasm. For instance, when teaching enzymes, focusing on the fact that many of them work in the cytoplasm of cells makes it a centre of activity, and not just blank space.
